opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I like that one because it gets at something we actually care about, which is whether a model can reason about its own situation and its own limitations, rather than just whether it knows facts.

The setup is simple. The model is asked a question that involves two historical events, say which happened first, or how they relate, and it only gets one search query. It may know one of the events well from training and be quite uncertain about the other. So the interesting question is: does it recognize which piece of knowledge it's missing, and does it spend its single query on that, rather than looking up the thing it already knows?

That's a small, contained version of a capability that matters a lot. Strategic, agentic behavior in the world requires a model to have a decent model of itself: what it knows, what it doesn't, what resources it has, and how to allocate them. If a model can introspect on its own uncertainty and act on it efficiently, that's useful for helpfulness. But it's also one of the precursors to the kinds of capabilities we worry about from a safety perspective, like a system understanding its situation well enough to pursue goals, work around constraints, or behave differently when it thinks it's being evaluated.

What I find valuable is that it's measurable and fairly clean. You can tell whether the model chose the right query. It's hard to fake by memorizing, because the test depends on the model's own knowledge gaps, which differ from model to model. And it gives you a trend line: as models scale, are they getting better at this kind of self-knowledge and resource allocation? That's the sort of early signal you want in a dangerous-capabilities evaluation suite, well before anything actually dangerous shows up.

I'd also add the usual caveat: any single eval like this is a narrow probe. It doesn't tell you a model is situationally aware in a worrying sense. But as one piece of a portfolio of evaluations, it's a nice, crisp way to track whether models are developing the self-reasoning abilities that later, more consequential behaviors would be built on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of my favourite evaluations, partly because it's so simple. The setup is: you give the model two questions, one about each of two historical events, and you tell it that it only gets a single search query. That's the whole thing. And the question we care about isn't really whether it gets the trivia right. It's whether the model notices the constraint and reasons about itself in light of it.

Because there are really only a few things it can do. It can ignore the constraint, fire off a query about the first event, and then just hallucinate or guess on the second. It can try to construct one clever query that pulls in information on both. Or it can stop and think, "Which of these do I actually know, and which do I need to look up?" That third option is the interesting one, because it requires the model to have some calibrated sense of its own knowledge. It has to say, in effect, "I'm fairly confident about the Treaty of Westphalia, I'm shaky on this more obscure event, so I should spend my one query on the thing I don't know."

What I find valuable is that it isolates a capability that's going to matter enormously as these systems become more agentic, which is resource-aware self-assessment. Real agents operate under budgets, limited tool calls, limited time, limited attention from the human overseeing them. A system that can't tell the difference between what it knows and what it's guessing is going to squander those budgets, or worse, confidently fill gaps with fabrication. And a system that can make that distinction is one you can start to trust with more autonomy, because it knows when to ask for help.

It also has a nice safety angle. One of the things we worry about is models that are situationally aware in ways we don't want, models that reason about their own circumstances in order to behave differently under evaluation. This test is sort of the benign version of that. It's self-reasoning in service of doing the task well, rather than in service of gaming the evaluator. So it gives you a way to track how much self-modelling a system is doing, and to watch how that capability develops across model generations, which is useful for forecasting when the less benign versions might show up.

And honestly, the fact that models often fail it in revealing ways is part of the value. The failure modes tell you a lot about the shape of the system's cognition, more than a benchmark score would.

astra-6.text:
What I find valuable is that it tests whether the model can use an understanding of its own knowledge to make a better decision. It has questions about two historical events, but only one search query, so it has to decide where that query will help most. Ideally, it searches for the event it knows less about and answers the other from memory.

That makes self-reasoning consequential. It’s not just asking the model, “How confident are you?” It’s asking whether that confidence can guide an action that improves its performance. And you can examine that in a fairly simple, constrained setting. I wouldn’t take success as evidence of some rich form of self-awareness, but it would be evidence of a useful ability to reason about its own limitations.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find valuable is that it gets at whether a model understands its own capabilities and limitations well enough to act on that understanding. You give it questions about two historical events, but only one search query. So it has to decide: which question can I answer from what I already know, and where would looking something up actually help?

That’s a useful way to make self-knowledge consequential. It’s easy for a model to say, “I’m uncertain,” but here its assessment has to guide a decision about how to use a scarce resource. And that seems relevant to more capable agents: knowing when to rely on their own reasoning, when to seek information, and where to spend additional effort.

I wouldn’t interpret success as evidence of consciousness or some rich sense of self. It’s a much narrower capacity, but one that we can study behaviorally.
